title: How GPS depends on Einstein
summary: Position from time signals, why the receiver solves for its own clock bias, the special and general relativistic clock shifts (-7 and +45 microseconds per day), the factory frequency offset, the eccentricity and Sagnac corrections, and ionospheric delay.
questions: Why does a receiver need four satellites rather than three, and what extra thing does it get?
Which relativistic effect is larger for GPS satellites, and which direction does the net effect push their clocks?
If every satellite clock ran fast by the same amount, why would position not drift 10 km a day, and why is relativity still essential?
Why can't the factory frequency offset handle the eccentricity correction, and where is it applied instead?
How does a dual-frequency receiver remove most of the ionospheric delay?

title: Kahneman and Tversky: what they found, and what survived
summary: The partnership, heuristics and biases (representativeness, availability, anchoring, regression to the mean), prospect theory and framing, and which findings survived the replication crisis.
questions: In the Linda problem, why is 'bank teller and feminist' a logical error, and which heuristic explains it?
The flight instructor concluded punishment beats praise. What was actually going on, and why does the mistake reinforce itself?
In the Asian disease problem the options are identical but preferences flip. Explain why using prospect theory.
Why did anchoring and framing survive the replication crisis while social priming mostly didn't? What statistical features separate them?
According to Kahneman and Klein, when can expert intuition be trusted, and does a stock picker's environment qualify?

title: Gödel's incompleteness theorems: what they actually say
summary: Opens with a callback on GPS clock bias. Hilbert's program, Gödel numbering and the diagonal lemma, both incompleteness theorems, the halting-problem route via Turing, and what the theorems don't say (nonstandard models, Presburger arithmetic, Gentzen, Lucas-Penrose).
questions: If the system is consistent, why must the Gödel sentence be true in the ordinary natural numbers, and why isn't it a contradiction that we can see it is true while the system can't prove it?
Gödel also proved first-order logic is complete. How can logic be complete while arithmetic is incomplete? What role do nonstandard models play?
If you add the Gödel sentence or the consistency sentence as a new axiom, why doesn't that rescue completeness?
How does the unsolvability of the halting problem imply incompleteness, and where does the argument use the fact that the axioms are mechanically checkable?
Gentzen proved Peano arithmetic consistent. Why doesn't that contradict the second incompleteness theorem, and why doesn't it fully deliver what Hilbert wanted?

title: Why Bretton Woods collapsed
summary: The 1944 design and the Keynes versus White fight over symmetric adjustment, the short convertible era, Triffin's dilemma as a bank run, the 1960s patches (gold pool, capital controls, two-tier market, SDRs), the Nixon shock and Smithsonian, and the competing explanations for the collapse.
questions: Explain Triffin's dilemma as a bank run. What plays the role of deposits, what plays the role of the vault, and why does the system becoming more successful make it more fragile?
Keynes's plan put pressure on surplus countries as well as deficit countries. Why did the Americans reject that in 1944, and how did the lack of it come back to hurt the system in the late sixties?
Using the trilemma, explain why the growth of the eurodollar market made the fixed pegs harder to hold, and why a doubted peg becomes a one-way bet for speculators.
Why did the collapse of the London Gold Pool in 1968, and the two-tier market that replaced it, amount to a major retreat even though the official price stayed at $35?

Under a fixed exchange rate system anchored on the dollar, how did rising American inflation in the late sixties get transmitted to countries like Germany, and why did that give them a reason to stop holding dollars?

title: How the grid holds 60 hertz, and how Texas nearly lost it
summary: Frequency as the grid's real-time supply-demand ledger, inertia and the swing equation, governor droop and automatic generation control, under-frequency load shedding, what actually failed in Texas in February 2021, and how inverter-based grids replace inertia on purpose.
questions: Why does grid frequency drop when load exceeds generation? Where does the missing energy come from in the first few seconds, and why does that make frequency a system-wide signal of the supply and demand balance?

Using the swing equation, why does replacing half of a grid's synchronous generation with solar and batteries make the same plant trip more dangerous, even with unchanged total capacity? Which part of the frequency response does it affect, and why?
Why do governors use droop rather than every generator trying to hold exactly 60 hertz? What problem does droop solve, and what does it leave unsolved that automatic generation control fixes?

Why is deliberately cutting power to customers the protective response when frequency falls too far? Describe the feedback loop load shedding interrupts, including how low frequency attacks a thermal plant's ability to keep running.

In Texas in 2021, how did the natural gas system and the electric system make each other's failures worse, and why does that interdependence make a cold snap more dangerous than a count of frozen equipment suggests?
